| `StudentHome.tsx` | 1318, 1324, 1470, 1690 | the `pendingSessionId` prop and state that exist only to feed it |
| `StudentHome.test.tsx` | 1258-1284 | the only place the limitation is currently written down |

## The one constraint

**Do not "fix" this by making the row stay mounted.** The row disappearing is the correct product behaviour — an answered opportunity is no longer an unanswered one — and `getUnansweredOutreachOpportunities` is shared. The choice is between deleting the dead code and documenting it honestly, not between those and resurrecting the spinner.

Note also that `isDisabled` on the same two buttons is **not** dead and must stay: it was measured working on the real components (`nativeDisabled=true` on sibling rows mid-flight). Only the `isLoading`/`pendingSessionId` pair is inert.

## Size and tier

One file. Either delete `pendingSessionId` and the two `isLoading` props and the state that feeds them (~15 lines across 4 sites), or move `StudentHome.test.tsx:1258-1284`'s caveat into the module doc (~5 lines). No write path changes either way — the `rsvps` upsert is untouched.

Suggested tier **STANDARD**: it is small and safe, but a deletion has no natural mutation that turns a test red, which is one of item 26's FAST preconditions.

## Suggested priority: low

1. **No user is harmed and none will report it.** The in-flight state is already legible through the row's disappearance and the sibling disable.
2. **Nothing is blocked on it.** No row cites it.
3. **The cost is a misleading comment in a file the next RSVP task will read.** That is the whole case for fixing it — an implementer who trusts `StudentHome.tsx:1321-1323` will believe the per-row spinner works.

It stops being deferrable the next time someone edits this control, because they will read the comment.

## Verification note

Found by `checker-reviewer` during GAM-304's HEAVY acceptance check and **confirmed by execution twice** — once by the worker, once independently by the checker in its own worktree. Line numbers re-checked at `4460dec` on `claude/gam-304-rsvp-write` on 2026-08-10.

**These line numbers refer to the GAM-304 branch, not to** `main` — GAM-304 has not merged as this is written. Re-verify after it lands.

The related acceptance criterion (GAM-304's packet criterion 7, "the **clicked** button shows `isLoading`") was graded **structurally unsatisfiable as written**. The worker asserted only the observable sibling-disable half and disclosed the rest rather than fabricating an assertion, which is the correct outcome; the criterion was defective, not the implementation.

issues.title: A failed RSVP save tells the user "Couldn't load this data" — read copy on a write path
issues.description:
When a student's or parent's RSVP fails to save, the banner tells them to check whether their data **loaded**:

> **Couldn't save your RSVP**
> Couldn't load this data. Check your connection and try again.

The title is right and the advice happens to still apply, so nobody is told a failed save succeeded. But the sentence describes the wrong operation, and it is the copy a real user hits on a configured deployment — the dominant failure mode, not an edge case.

## Why it happens

`extractRsvpErrorMessage` (`StudentHome.tsx:963`, `ParentHome.tsx:1017`) forwards `error.message` verbatim for anything matching `isSupabaseLoaderError`. For every rejection except one, `toLoaderError` (`loader.ts:120`) has already replaced that message with the module-wide constant:

```ts
const DEFAULT_LOADER_ERROR_MESSAGE =
  "Couldn't load this data. Check your connection and try again.";
```

That constant is correct for the reads it was written for (`loader.ts:88-93` explains the fixed-copy rule, and it is deliberate DES-16 policy, not an oversight). It is simply the wrong verb for a write, and the RSVP controls are the first write path to reuse it.

The passthrough itself is **not** the bug and must be kept: it is what lets `SupabaseNotConfiguredError`'s hand-authored copy reach the banner (`loader.ts:105-119`), which is the single exception `toLoaderError` carves out and which GAM-304's acceptance criterion 1 exists to prove.

## Where it lives

| File | Line | What it does |
| -- | -- | -- |
| `StudentHome.tsx` | 963-967 | `extractRsvpErrorMessage`, forwards the loader message |
| `StudentHome.tsx` | 1582 | `title="Couldn't save your RSVP"` — the correct half |
| `ParentHome.tsx` | 1017-1021 | the same function, independently reimplemented |
| `loader.ts` | 93 | `DEFAULT_LOADER_ERROR_MESSAGE`, the read-flavoured string |

## The one constraint

`src/lib/supabase/loader.ts` **is the root cause and is the wrong place to fix it.** Changing `DEFAULT_LOADER_ERROR_MESSAGE` would re-word every read failure across the app to say "save". Fix at the call site, in the two home files, by branching on `error.code` or by reserving the passthrough for the not-configured message only.

Keep the `SupabaseNotConfiguredError` passthrough working — it is pinned by a test that asserts the "Supabase isn't configured yet" copy reaches the banner with **no injected seam**. Breaking it silently re-opens the packet defect GAM-304's worker found by execution.

`extractRsvpErrorMessage` is duplicated in both files on purpose (the files' established independent-reimplementation convention, like `applyRsvpOverride`/`withLocalRsvpOverride`). Change both; do not extract a shared helper without a ruling.

## Size and tier

Two files, one function each, display strings only. No write path, no schema, no signature another module imports.

Suggested tier **FAST**: a named mutation exists that turns it red — restore the unconditional passthrough and the new save-copy assertion fails.

## Suggested priority: medium urgency, very low cost

1. **A user can actually see this one**, unlike the other two GAM-304 follow-ups. It needs only a failed write on a configured deployment.
2. **Nobody has hit it yet.** Public go-live is still an unopened human gate (`GAM-80`/T070) and the MIG-06 cutover (`GAM-75`/T065) is Backlog — but a production database does exist, so confirm rather than assume.
3. **Nothing is blocked on it**, and the fix is a few display strings.

It stops being deferrable at go-live, alongside the rest of the DES-16 copy pass.

## Verification note

Found by `checker-reviewer` during GAM-304's HEAVY acceptance check, by rendering the real banner for a generic `SupabaseLoaderError` rather than by reading the code:

```
P3 BANNER="Couldn't save your RSVPCouldn't load this data. Check your connection and try again.Dismiss"
```

Graded **MINOR, not MAJOR**, on the explicit ground that the title is correct and no user is told a failed save succeeded.

Independently re-checked at `4460dec` on `claude/gam-304-rsvp-write` on 2026-08-10: `extractRsvpErrorMessage` at `StudentHome.tsx:963` and `ParentHome.tsx:1017` both forward `error.message`; `loader.ts:120` sets it to `DEFAULT_LOADER_ERROR_MESSAGE` for every rejection except `SupabaseNotConfiguredError`; the banner title at `StudentHome.tsx:1582` reads "Couldn't save your RSVP".

**These line numbers refer to the GAM-304 branch, not to** `main` — GAM-304 has not merged as this is written. Re-verify after it lands.

issues.title: ArrowDown opens the Next-up row's `aria-disabled` MoreMenu mid-write, while the mouse is correctly blocked
issues.description:
While an RSVP write is in flight, the Next-up row's "..." menu is disabled for the mouse and open to the keyboard. Clicking the trigger does nothing (correct); pressing **ArrowDown** on it opens the menu anyway.

No data is at risk. The menu's action is guarded a second time, and a write launched from the opened menu is swallowed — measured, the write count stayed at **1**. The window is sub-second. What is wrong is that the same control answers two input methods differently, which is an accessibility consistency defect rather than a correctness one.

## Why it happens

The row uses `MoreMenu`'s menu-level `isDisabled`, which `astryx-api.md:4822` documents as disabling *the trigger*. That maps to `Button`'s disabled handling, and `@astryxdesign/core`'s `Button` only suppresses **Enter and Space** (`Button.js:372-380`); every other key is forwarded to `DropdownMenu`'s `handleButtonKeyDown`, which opens on ArrowDown. Mouse clicks are stopped earlier (`Button.js:355` early-returns before `props.onClick`), hence the asymmetry.

So `isDisabled` on this component means "not clickable", not "not operable".

## Where it lives

| File | Line | What it does |
| -- | -- | -- |
| `StudentHome.tsx` | 1301 | the `MoreMenu` on a Next-up row |
| `StudentHome.tsx` | 1283-1286 | the comment choosing the menu-level prop, and why |
| `node_modules/@astryxdesign/core/dist/Button/Button.js` | 355, 372-380 | click blocked, ArrowDown forwarded |

## The one constraint

**Two fixes, and they are not equivalent.** Per-entry `DropdownMenuOption.isDisabled` disables the *action* and would not have this gap, but it changes what the user sees: the menu opens and shows an unavailable item, rather than the row appearing inert. The menu-level prop was chosen deliberately to match "every other control disables while any write is in flight", so swapping it is a UX decision, not a refactor.

The alternative is to leave the code and file the keydown composition upstream against `@astryxdesign/core`.

Do **not** reach for a native `disabled` attribute. The trigger currently renders `aria-disabled="true"` with `tabIndex=0`, which was measured to preserve focus order and create no focus trap; a native `disabled` would remove it from the tab sequence and is the worse accessibility outcome.

## Size and tier

One prop on one component, or one upstream bug report. No write path, no schema.

Suggested tier **FAST** if the decision is "swap to the per-entry prop" — but the decision itself is the work, and item 2 binds any Astryx prop to `docs/swarm/astryx-api.md`.

## Suggested priority: low

1. **No data risk, measured.** The `isRsvpSubmitting` guard held and the concurrency guard kept the write count at 1 even when the menu was opened by keyboard and its item activated.
2. **The window is the duration of one network write**, and only a keyboard user who presses ArrowDown during it is affected.
3. **Nothing is blocked on it.**

Against that: item 15 makes accessibility a shipping requirement and keyboard path failures on core flows a BLOCKER. This is not a keyboard *failure* — the keyboard user gets more access, not less, and cannot corrupt anything — so it does not meet that bar. Worth resolving in the same pass as the next Astryx accessibility review rather than on its own.

## Verification note

Found by `checker-reviewer` during GAM-304's HEAVY acceptance check. It is exactly the trade-off GAM-304's packet named in its own least-confident decision #2 (`docs/swarm/active/GAM-304-worker-packet.md:500-507`) — which is item 19d working as intended: the author declared the doubt, and the check found the thing the doubt predicted.

Measured in the DOM, not read from source: mouse click → `aria-expanded=false` (blocked); ArrowDown → `aria-expanded=true` (opens); trigger renders `aria-disabled="true"`, `nativeDisabled=false`, `tabIndex=0`, `focusable=true`.

The checker also recorded that its *first* probe reported "menu opened" for the mouse path and that this was a **false positive** — the `role="menu"` popover node is always present in the jsdom DOM, so `aria-expanded` is the real signal. That correction is kept here rather than deleted, because it is the evidence the check actually happened.

Line numbers re-checked at `4460dec` on `claude/gam-304-rsvp-write` on 2026-08-10. **They refer to the GAM-304 branch, not to** `main` — GAM-304 has not merged as this is written.

issues.title: The opus orchestrator runs the gates itself: 238 Bash calls, and `checker-tests` is pinned haiku to do exactly that
issues.description:
A HEAVY row consumes roughly $37-45 notional end to end. The largest single reducible share is not the model tiering, the turn cap or the gate rounds — it is the orchestrator personally running `npm ci`, `tsc`, `vitest`, `eslint`, git and mutation replays on **opus**, while `checker-tests` sits pinned to **haiku** with the charter *"runs lint, typecheck, tests, and build."*

Measured across four [GAM-304](https://linear.app/gamitch/issue/GAM-304/t809-studenthomes-sign-up-cant-go-control-writes-nothing-and-says) runs, orchestrator Bash calls track consumption almost linearly.

## Why it is worth fixing

**These are notional figures, not spend.** The dispatch workflow authenticates with `claude_code_oauth_token`, so runs draw on the owner's subscription and `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` is empty; `total_cost_usd` prices each run's tokens at API list rates and no invoice follows. They are kept because they are the only quantitative signal — subscription consumption is exposed as a number nowhere, and this one is proportional to tokens weighted by model tier.

What they measure is **capacity**, and capacity is what actually runs out. This project has stalled on usage windows repeatedly; several scheduled prompts in the account open with *"usage window has reset"* and *"Usage limit should have reset."* At $37-45 per HEAVY row, the practical question is how many rows fit in a window before work stops — and the owner raised exactly that concern.

## Why it happens

Nothing tells the orchestrator to delegate mechanical execution, so it does it inline. It is also the cheapest thing to write and the hardest to notice, because every individual command looks trivial — the cost is in 238 of them each returning output into a growing opus context.

The second half is duplicated verification. Item 26 assigns orchestrator mutation-replay to **STANDARD** (*"worker implements, orchestrator replays the mutation. No separate checker round"*) and gives **HEAVY** a separate checker instead. Run 31385764526 did both: the orchestrator re-ran all six gates *and* replayed criterion 2's mutation in its own worktree, then dispatched `checker-reviewer` (opus) to attack the same work. Two opus passes over one diff.

## Where it lives

| File | Line | What it does |
| -- | -- | -- |
| `.claude/agents/checker-tests.md` | frontmatter | `model: haiku`, `tools: Read, Bash, Glob, Grep` — the agent built for this, currently unused by the dispatch path |
| `docs/swarm/constitution.md` | 337-340 | item 26 STANDARD: orchestrator replays the mutation, no separate checker |
| `docs/swarm/constitution.md` | 342-351 | item 26 HEAVY: packet + premise gate + worker + checker |
| `.github/workflows/claude-linear-dispatch.yml` | 226-275 | the `--model` block, where the orchestrator's tier is set and this trade-off is now noted |

Measured, every figure from the runs' own `result` objects:

| Run | Turns | Wall | Bash | Notional | Shape |
| -- | -- | -- | -- | -- | -- |
| 31357084288 | 64 | 22 min | — | **$8.52** | one gate subagent |
| 31385764526 | 54 | 59 min | **238** | **$28.58** | worker + orchestrator re-verification + checker |
| 31391626696 | 65 | 27 min | **91** | **$8.61** | resume, checker only |

The resume is the control. It had *more* turns than the expensive run (65 vs 54) and consumed a third as much, with a third the Bash calls. Turn count is not the driver; orchestrator-executed shell work is.

## The one constraint

**This must not reduce verification, and item 26 says so in terms:** *"Verification is not reduced — the mutation is run and its real red output reported… What is removed is coordination, not evidence."* The proposal is to move mechanical *execution* to a cheaper tier, never to skip it.

Two things must survive any change:

* **Item 21's existence check stays with the orchestrator.** *"'Clean' and 'committed' are different claims."* That check is cheap, and T142 is the recorded case of it being assumed rather than verified — work that was real, measured and entirely uncommitted.
* **The orchestrator's independent replay is a control against a lying worker**, not decoration. On run 31385764526 it found nothing the checker did not later confirm, but that is one sample and the wrong lesson to draw from it. The safer split is: orchestrator verifies *existence and boundary* (cheap, and its own job), `checker-tests` on haiku *executes* the gates, `checker-reviewer` on opus does the *judgement*. Nobody stops running anything.

## Size and tier

A prompt change plus a delegation convention. No source, no schema, no write path. The measurement to prove it is already available: re-run a HEAVY row and compare orchestrator Bash count and `total_cost_usd` against the three rows above.

Tier unjudged, because item 28c makes that the picker's first act.

## Suggested priority: medium urgency, low cost

Worth doing before the next batch of HEAVY rows, not before the next single one.

1. **Nothing is broken.** Every run listed above produced correct work, and the HEAVY chain caught a real packet defect at the worker stage. This is efficiency, not correctness, and it should not jump ahead of `GAM-314` or `GAM-317`, which are correctness and process failures.
2. **Nothing is blocked on it.** No row cites this.

It stops being deferrable when a usage window interrupts work mid-row — the failure mode this project has already hit more than once, and the one that turns an efficiency issue into a scheduling one.

## Verification note

Re-checked against `main` (`49096db`) on 2026-08-10. Every figure is quoted from a run's own `result` object or from a transcript tool-count, not estimated.

* **Two of the five** [GAM-304](https://linear.app/gamitch/issue/GAM-304/t809-studenthomes-sign-up-cant-go-control-writes-nothing-and-says) **runs are excluded from the table on purpose.** Run 31349834462 ($9.16) and run 31358757094 (unmeasured — its artifact was lost to the cancellation bug since fixed) both delivered nothing, so including them would overstate the steady-state cost of a HEAVY row. They are why the total consumed on [GAM-304](https://linear.app/gamitch/issue/GAM-304/t809-studenthomes-sign-up-cant-go-control-writes-nothing-and-says) is ~$85 rather than ~$46.
* **The causal claim is a correlation across three runs, not an experiment.** Bash-calls-on-opus tracks consumption in this sample, and the mechanism is plausible (each result enlarges an opus context). It has not been isolated — the expensive run also carried the largest context and two subagents. Measure before assuming the saving is the full difference.

issues.title: Three unscoped Linear git automations are live where item 28g asked for one — `start → In Progress` is the rule that moved GAM-304 backwards
issues.description:
Merging a pull request whose branch is named after an issue moves that issue,
whatever the PR body says. On 2026-08-10 that closed `GAM-304` four times from
branches carrying none of its work, and on the fifth — the PR that actually
fixed it, `Closes GAM-304` on body line 1 — it moved the issue *backwards* from
`In Review` to `In Progress`. The owner closed it by hand.

Both behaviours come from the same place: team `GAM` has **three** git
automations enabled, and all three are unscoped.

```
event=start   targetBranch=null (ANY) -> In Progress (started)
event=review  targetBranch=null (ANY) -> In Review   (started)
event=merge   targetBranch=null (ANY) -> Done        (completed)
```

Constitution item 28g asked the owner to enable one of these, *PR merged →**
**Done*. Three are on, and the other two are recorded nowhere.

## Why it is worth fixing

`Done` is the one state nobody re-reads. An issue that reaches it silently is
this tracker's worst failure mode, and `GAM-304` reached it four times on the
strength of a substring in a branch name. It stayed closed for twenty seconds
on the first occasion and was rescued by an unrelated move back to `Todo`.

The second failure is subtler and cost real owner time: `start → In Progress`
outranks `merge → Done` when any other linked PR is still open, so the merge of
an issue's own fix can move it backwards. That is what happened at 14:00:04Z,
with `#142` still open.

Nothing is blocked on this. Every issue with more than one linked PR is
exposed, and that is now common.

## Why it happens

Linear puts a PR in an issue's linked set when the branch name carries the
identifier, when the body carries a magic word, and — measured, though
confounded with the negated-magic-word case — when the title carries the
identifier. The three automations then compute the issue's state from the
**aggregate** of that set rather than from the merge event, so `merge → Done`
fires only when the merging PR is the last one open.

`GAM-315` fixes the documentation side of this: it corrects item 28f, which
claimed a branch-name identifier "links only", and adds a convention keeping
mention-branches out of the linked set. **That is a mitigation, not a fix.** It
depends on every future agent naming branches correctly. Scoping or disabling
the automations is the only control that does not.

## Where it lives

| Where | What |
| -- | -- |
| Linear → Settings → Team `GAM` → Integrations → GitHub → pull request automation | The three rules above. Not in the repository. |
| `docs/swarm/constitution.md` item 28g | Asked for one automation; corrected by GAM-315 to record all three |
| `docs/swarm/constitution.md` item 28f | The "links only" claim GAM-315 removes |

Reproduce the configuration without opening the UI — `LINEAR_API_KEY` is
already what `scripts/linear/*.mjs` use:

```js
import { gql } from './scripts/linear/client.mjs';
await gql('{ teams(first:5){ nodes{ key gitAutomationStates(first:30){ nodes{ event targetBranch{ id branchPattern isRegex } state{ name type } } } } } }');
```

## The one constraint

`targetBranch` **cannot express this.** It scopes the PR's *base* branch — the
branch being merged into — not its head. Every PR here targets `main`, so no
`targetBranch` pattern can distinguish a branch that does an issue's work from
one that merely mentions it. Do not reach for it as the fix.

That leaves three real options, and the choice is a judgement about which
failure is cheaper:

1. **Disable** `start → In Progress`**.** Stops the backwards move. Does not stop a
   wrong close, and gives up automatic `In Progress` on first push.
2. **Disable** `merge → Done`**.** Stops every wrong close. Also stops every right
   one — issues sit in `In Review` until closed by hand, which is what item 28e
   already asks agents to do, so the cost falls on the owner rather than on
   correctness.
3. **Leave all three on** and rely on GAM-315's branch-naming convention. Zero
   setup, and it fails the first time an agent names a branch carelessly.

## Size and tier

No repository change. One decision and a few clicks in Linear settings, plus a
one-line update to item 28g afterwards to record what was chosen. `gate/human`:
no agent may change a workspace setting, and no machine may close this row.

## Suggested priority

**Medium urgency, near-zero cost — but decide it, do not let it sit.**

GAM-315's documentation fix lands first and removes the surprise, which is the
part that actually hurt. After that this is a defence-in-depth question rather
than a live bug, so it can wait weeks.

It stops being deferrable the first time an agent needs a branch that mentions
an issue it is not implementing and gets the naming wrong — which has already
happened four times in one day, before the convention existed to be got wrong.

Recommendation: **option 1, disable** `start → In Progress`**.** It removes the
failure that cost owner time and could not have been caught by reading, keeps
automatic closing (which agents rely on under item 28e/28f), and leaves the
wrong-close risk to the naming convention, where a mistake is visible in the
branch name rather than invisible in a state history.

## Verification note

Measured 2026-08-10 against `main` `43d99c7`. The automation configuration is
**read from Linear's** `gitAutomationStates`, not inferred from behaviour — the
filing that raised this (GAM-315) listed "whether the automation is scoped or
global" as unverified, and it is now answered: unscoped.

* The aggregate-state hypothesis was GAM-315's, marked unverified. It is
  confirmed: `merge → Done` fired on each of #138, #139, #140, #141, #144 (each
  the last open linked PR at its merge) and not on #143, the only merge with
  another linked PR open.
* **Correction to GAM-315's own figures.** It states four wrong closes; there
  are five. Of GAM-304's seven linked PRs, six intended no magic word and three
  contain no magic-word token at all.
* **Unverified, deliberately.** Whether a PR *title* identifier links on its
  own cannot be separated from the negated-magic-word case by any data in this
  repository — the only two candidate PRs (#132, #131) carry a magic-word token
  in the body. Settling it means firing a live automation against the tracker,
  and it changes no prescription, so it was not run.
* **Untested channels.** Whether a commit message or a PR comment can create a
  link was not measured. If either can, the branch-naming convention has a hole
  and option 3 is weaker than it looks.

issues.title: AGENTS.md tells every agent a branch-name identifier does not close its issue — measured, it closes
issues.description:
`AGENTS.md` — the file a Codex agent reads at startup — tells it that putting an issue identifier in a branch name or PR title is safe, because it "links but does **not** close". Measured on 2026-08-10, it closes. An agent that trusts line 37 and names an investigation branch `claude/gam-nnn-*` will silently close an issue it never worked on, and `Done` is the one state nobody re-reads.

This is the same defect [GAM-315](https://linear.app/gamitch/issue/GAM-315/any-branch-named-claudegam-nnn-closes-that-issue-on-merge-item-28f) is fixing in `constitution.md` item 28f. **A repo-wide grep finds exactly two live assertions of the falsified mechanism:** `constitution.md:467`**, which GAM-315 covers, and** `AGENTS.md:37`**, which it does not.** Correcting one and leaving the other is the documentation drift that produced this bug in the first place.

## Why it is worth fixing

Nobody is harmed today — no user surface is involved. The exposure is to agents, and it is live: four of GAM-304's seven linked pull requests were CI and salvage work that closed it anyway, four separate times.

`AGENTS.md` is the higher-risk of the two files, not the lower. It is the **entry point**: an agent reads it before it reads the constitution, and it is written as terse operational instructions rather than as reasoning, so there is nothing in the surrounding text to prompt a second look.

A second, quieter claim on `AGENTS.md:30` — that the branch name links "from the first push" — is **unmeasured**. GAM-315's packet withdrew exactly that claim from its own text after a premise gate found no evidence for it, and a later attempt to measure it was refuted for want of a positive control. It should not stand here while it is struck there.

## Why it happens

Team `GAM` has three unscoped Linear git automations, of which `merge → Done` is one (read from `gitAutomationStates`, not inferred). Linear links a PR to an issue when the identifier appears in the branch name or title, so the automation fires on any such merge and the PR body never enters into it. Omitting the `Closes` magic word protects nothing.

`AGENTS.md:36-37` describes Linear's magic-word feature accurately in isolation. What it does not account for is the team automation — which `constitution.md` item 28g asks the owner to enable, and which is enabled.

## Where it lives

| File | Line | What it says | Status |
| -- | -- | -- | -- |
| `AGENTS.md` | 36-37 | "An identifier in the title or branch links but does **not** close." | **False** — measured, it closes |
| `AGENTS.md` | 30 | "Linear links on the identifier in the branch name, so the issue connects from the first push" | **Unmeasured** — the timing half; struck in GAM-315's packet |
| `AGENTS.md` | 190-192 | Reserves this file to "the primary orchestrator"; names no boss role | The authority question below |

## The one constraint

**Do not fix this by dropping identifiers from branch names**, and do not weaken `AGENTS.md:29` for real implementation work. That convention is load-bearing — a session-scoped branch name looks reserved and is not, and two sessions once worked one mutable ref because of it. GAM-315 carries the same constraint.

**Wait for GAM-315.** This correction must say the same thing item 28f ends up saying, and 28f is not written yet — its premise gate has returned REVISE three times and the wording is with the owner. Landing this first means guessing at text that is still moving, and then reconciling two files instead of one. Sequence it after.

## The authority question this row exists to surface

`AGENTS.md:190-192` reserves the file to "the primary orchestrator" and names **no boss role**. `constitution.md:22-24` reserves the constitution to `boss-architect` / `boss-arbiter`. So the agent authorized to write the corrected wording in item 28f is the one agent not clearly authorized to copy it into `AGENTS.md`.

That is why this is a separate row rather than a fourth file on GAM-315's packet: **a task packet may not settle an authority question by assuming it.** Two ways to close it, and the choice is the owner's:

1. **Fold it into GAM-315** — add `AGENTS.md` to that packet's Allowed Files and let `boss-architect` make both edits together, guaranteeing they agree. Cheapest, and closes this row unstarted.
2. **Keep it separate** — the orchestrator applies it after item 28f lands, under its own `AGENTS.md` ownership. Slower, and risks the two files drifting.

Recommendation: **option 1**, unless the owner wants the authority boundary stated explicitly in the constitution first.

## Size and tier

Two sentences in one file, no code, no user surface. **STANDARD** under item 26, not FAST: FAST requires "a named mutation exists that turns a test red", and a prose correction has no test to redden, so the evidence FAST refuses to give up cannot be produced in this form. Not HEAVY — no write path, no RLS, auth, migration or metric SQL, and the *premise* has already had three gate rounds on GAM-315.

## Suggested priority

**Low urgency, near-zero cost, but do not lose it — and do it in the same breath as GAM-315.**

* **Who is affected today:** agents only, not users. No student, parent or coach can reach this.
* **Has anyone seen it:** yes, four times on GAM-304 in one day — though via the constitution and branch convention rather than by an agent citing `AGENTS.md:37` specifically.
* **What it blocks:** nothing.
* **What it costs:** two sentences.
* **When it stops being deferrable:** **the moment item 28f is corrected.** From then on the repository states two contradictory things about the same mechanism, in its two highest-authority documents, and the false one is in the file read first.

## Verification note

Verified 2026-08-10 against current `main` (`43d99c7`); `git diff --stat origin/main -- AGENTS.md` is empty on the working branch, so these line numbers are `main`'s.

* `AGENTS.md:36-37` and `:30` quoted verbatim above from `sed -n '28,38p'`. Both confirmed independently by two `checker-premise` runs on opus.
* The three unscoped automations were read from Linear's `gitAutomationStates` API by two separate agent runs in different containers, reaching identical results — not inferred from behaviour.
* **Correction to how this was nearly filed.** The run that opened this row first claimed to have *measured* that a branch name does not link on push, from an identifier-carrying branch pushed twice with no PR and an empty `attachments` array. Gate round 3 refuted it: the issue was already `In Progress`, so `start → In Progress` would have been a no-op and unobservable; and a sweep of the first 40 GAM issues found 13 attachments, all `sourceType: "github"` with `/pull/` URLs and none of branch type, so an empty array is uninformative. **The claim is withdrawn** and `AGENTS.md:30` is listed above as unmeasured rather than as false. The error is kept here because it is the third unmeasured claim this topic has produced in three gate rounds, which is itself the argument for the row.

---

| Provenance |  |
| -- | -- |
| Filed by | GAM-315 dispatch run 2, orchestrator, 2026-08-10 |
| Under | Constitution item 20 (a deliberate deferral files a task, not a comment) |
| Found by | `checker-premise` round 3 on the GAM-315 packet — MAJOR finding 3 |
| Parent | GAM-315 — corrects the same claim in `constitution.md:467` |
| Sibling | GAM-322 — the Linear-side automation decision (`gate/human`) |
| Scope record | `docs/swarm/active/GAM-315-packet.md` § "Deliberately NOT in scope" |

issues.title: Three documents state the protected-files rule and all three disagree — on who is bound, who owns, and which paths
issues.description:
An agent that wants to know whether it may edit a file has three places to look and gets three different answers. The disagreement already cost a decision: a `GAM-315` run needed to correct one sentence in `AGENTS.md`, could not establish whether it was allowed to, and stopped to ask the owner.

## The three statements, verbatim

`docs/swarm/constitution.md:22-33` — binding under item 1:

> Only the following agents may modify this constitution: `boss-architect`, `boss-arbiter`
>
> Workers may not edit: `constitution.md`, `task-ledger.md`, `verification-log.md`, `dispute-log.md`, `.claude/agents/`, `.claude/skills/`, `.claude/settings.json`

`AGENTS.md:190-192` — the file agents read at startup:

> Workers **and checkers** must not edit `.claude/**`, `docs/swarm/**`, this `AGENTS.md`, **workflow files**, or project governance records. **The primary orchestrator** owns those records.

`SWARM-QUICKSTART.md:189` — the Claude-side reference:

> Workers cannot edit `.claude/`, `docs/swarm/`, or any workflow files.

## Where they diverge

|  | constitution | `AGENTS.md` | `SWARM-QUICKSTART.md` |
| -- | -- | -- | -- |
| **Who is bound** | workers | workers **and checkers** | workers |
| **Who owns** | `boss-architect` / `boss-arbiter` (of the constitution) | **the primary orchestrator** (of everything listed) | silent |
| `.claude/` | three named paths | **all of it** | all of it |
| `docs/swarm/` | four named files | **all of it** | all of it |
| `.github/workflows/` | **not listed** | protected | protected |
| `AGENTS.md` itself | **not listed** | protected | not mentioned |

Two of the three are **broader** than the binding document, and the middle one names a **different owner**.

## Why it is worth fixing

The owner-role conflict is the one with teeth. `AGENTS.md` assigns its own file to "the primary orchestrator"; the constitution assigns constitutional text to `boss-architect`. When one sentence must be corrected in both files at once — exactly `GAM-315`'s situation — **the agent authorised to write one half is the agent not clearly authorised to write the other**. The run behaved correctly: it refused to assume, filed `GAM-323`, and escalated. That is the right outcome and it cost a round trip.

The breadth conflict is quieter and more corrosive. An agent reading `AGENTS.md` believes `docs/swarm/**` is off-limits entirely; the constitution protects four files in it. Every routine write to `docs/swarm/active/` — packets, run logs, gate verdicts, which the dispatch prompt now *requires* — looks forbidden under one document and is plainly fine under another. Agents that follow the strictest reading do less than they may; agents that follow the constitution look like they are breaking a rule.

## Why it happens

Item 3 says rules live in one place. This rule lives in three, none of which points at the others, and each was written for a different reader at a different time — the constitution for the swarm, `AGENTS.md` for Codex, `SWARM-QUICKSTART.md` as a template guide that has never been updated since import. Three copies of a rule is a drift generator, and this is what drift looks like after a few weeks.

## The one constraint

**"Harmonize to the constitution" cannot mean copying the constitution's list into the other two — that would loosen real protections.** The constitution does not list `.github/workflows/`, `AGENTS.md`, or `docs/swarm/` as a whole, and does not bind checkers. Deleting those from the other files would silently permit things nobody has decided to permit.

So the work is **two decisions, in order**:

1. **What should actually be protected, and from whom?** Should the constitution *expand* to cover workflow files, `AGENTS.md` and checkers? That is a real change, not a transcription.
2. **Then, how is it stated once?** Almost certainly: the constitution holds the complete list, and `AGENTS.md` / `SWARM-QUICKSTART.md` point at it instead of restating it. Synchronising three copies just resets the clock on the same drift.

Second trap: `AGENTS.md`'s "project governance records" is undefined. Whatever replaces it must name paths, or it will be read three ways again.

## Where it lives

| File | Line | What it does |
| -- | -- | -- |
| `docs/swarm/constitution.md` | 22-33 | Authority Boundaries — the binding statement |
| `AGENTS.md` | 190-192 | broader list, different owner, binds checkers too |
| `SWARM-QUICKSTART.md` | 189-198 | third copy; already carries a warning that it disagrees, added 2026-08-10 |

## Size and tier

A constitution amendment plus two files reduced to pointers. No code, no schema, no user surface. Constitution edits are `boss-architect` / `boss-arbiter` only (the very rule at issue).

Tier unjudged, because item 28c makes that the picker's first act. It cannot be FAST as item 26 defines it — no test covers prose, so no named mutation can turn one red.

## Suggested priority: medium urgency, low cost

Worth doing before the next packet needs a file that sits in the gap.

1. **It has already cost one escalation and one owner ruling**, on `GAM-315` / `GAM-323`, and the ruling was explicitly scoped to that packet so the next one must ask again.
2. **Nothing is blocked on it**, but it silently taxes every packet that touches a governance file — and the dispatch prompt now *requires* writes to `docs/swarm/active/`, which one document reads as forbidden.

It stops being deferrable the next time an agent must edit a file in the gap and has to escalate to find out whether it may.

## Verification note

All three quotations read from `main` (`43d99c7`) on 2026-08-10, not recalled.

* **This session is the worked example.** `.github/workflows/claude-linear-dispatch.yml` was edited five times by an orchestrator. Under `AGENTS.md` workflow files are protected but the prohibition names workers and checkers, which an orchestrator is not; under the constitution the path is not listed at all. **So no rule was broken** — but establishing that took reading three documents mid-task, which is the cost this row is about.
* **Not established: whether the constitution's narrower list is deliberate or an omission.** It may have been written before workflow files existed in this repo. Whoever picks this up should check the git history of Authority Boundaries before assuming the gap is accidental — the answer changes whether decision 1 is an expansion or a correction.
